summary:
Lara is a 20-year-old female presenting with a BMI of 28.1, following a high-carbohydrate, low-fat diet rated 3 out of 10 for quality with a volume of 4 out of 10. She does no structured cardio or resistance training and walks 2,000 to 5,000 steps a day. She takes sertraline, guanfacine, melatonin and the combined oral contraceptive pill. She reports joint pain and stiffness, mainly in her hands, bloating and digestive discomfort on a background of long-standing IBS, frequent infections, daytime fatigue, eczema and jawline acne, night sweats and hot flushes, recurrent thrush and urinary infections, and a weight gain of more than 20 kilograms over the past year. Her goals are to reduce stress and anxiety, improve digestion and gut health, and improve her energy. She has hypermobility, is neurodivergent, had a pelvic MRI that found no endometriosis, and believes she caught glandular fever when she started university last September.

There is no finding in this report that needs to go to her GP as an emergency, and it is worth saying that first, because the year she describes would make anyone wonder. Her thyroid is working well, with the active hormone Free T3 at a healthy 5.67 and both thyroid antibodies negative, so an underactive thyroid is not the cause of the weight gain or the tiredness. Her kidneys are in excellent shape: cystatin C, the filtration marker that is not skewed by muscle mass, gives an eGFR of 129, and there is no protein leaking into the urine. Her full blood count is good, with a haemoglobin of 135 despite heavy periods, so she is not anaemic. The autoimmune screen matters enormously for someone with new hand joint pain and a raised inflammatory marker, and every part of it is negative: rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP (the most specific antibody for rheumatoid arthritis), antinuclear antibodies, complement C4, the coeliac antibody and both thyroid antibodies. The IL-17 family of inflammatory messengers, which drive psoriasis-type joint disease, are all low. Rheumatoid arthritis and lupus are therefore unlikely explanations for her hands, and hypermobility becomes the most probable one. Her lipoprotein (a), the inherited cholesterol particle that cannot be changed by lifestyle, is within the ideal range, which means everything wrong with her cholesterol is acquired and fixable. Every cancer screening marker is normal, including CA 125, which also rises with endometriosis and sits low here in keeping with her MRI. The Epstein-Barr antibodies confirm what she suspected: EBNA IgG and VCA IgG are strongly positive and VCA IgM is negative, which is the fingerprint of glandular fever that has passed. Fatigue after glandular fever can genuinely last a year, and it is a fair contributor to her daytime tiredness.

The central finding is insulin resistance, and almost everything else in this report is downstream of it. Insulin is the hormone that moves sugar out of the blood after a meal. Her fasting insulin is 151 pmol/L, which is 21.8 mIU/L against an ideal of 8 or below, and her C-peptide, a steadier measure of how hard the pancreas is working, is 3.28 against an ideal of 2.5. Her glucose is 5.21 and her HbA1c 38, both inside the laboratory range but above ideal, and putting glucose and insulin together gives a HOMA-IR of 5.0, where 1.5 or below is ideal. In plain terms, her body is producing three times the insulin it should need to keep her blood sugar where it is. Adiponectin, a hormone made by fat tissue that keeps the body sensitive to insulin, is 2.07 against a lower limit of 3.81, and it falls as visceral fat rises. Insulin at this level is a fat-storage signal, an appetite signal and an inflammatory signal all at once. It explains 20 kilograms in a year far better than eating habits do, it drives jawline acne through its effect on the skin, it lowers HDL and raises triglycerides, and it keeps her sex hormone binding globulin lower than it should be on the pill. At 20, with a normal uric acid, ideal urine albumin and no damage anywhere, this is entirely reversible, and reversing it is the plan.

Her cholesterol is the first consequence. Total cholesterol is 5.61 against a limit of 5.0 and LDL, the cholesterol in the particles that deposit in artery walls, is 3.81 against a limit of 3.0. The number that counts best is apolipoprotein B, which counts the artery-damaging particles themselves: at 1.33 g/L it is well above the ideal of 0.8. HDL, the protective particle, is 1.15 against a limit of 1.55, and the ApoB to ApoA-I ratio of 1.19 is double the ideal for a woman. The good news inside this is that small dense LDL, the most harmful form, is only slightly above ideal, and Lp(a) is fine. Put together, her Cardiovascular Risk Score, a TrueVitals index from 0 to 100 that scores the lipids, inflammation and blood sugar without any age term, comes out at 85, where 20 or below is ideal. That is a high score, and it should be read alongside the fact that her actual chance of a heart event in the next ten years is very low because she is 20: the score measures the risk being built, and at 20 there is time to unbuild it. This is the lipid signature of insulin resistance and the combined pill, not an inherited cholesterol disorder, and it responds to weight loss, resistance training and less refined carbohydrate more reliably than to anything else. Her GP may also wish to review the type of contraception in light of the cholesterol and the clotting risk of oestrogen, though her D-dimer is normal.

Her liver is showing the earliest sign of the same process. GGT, the liver enzyme most sensitive to metabolic strain, is 47.9 against a limit of 42, and ALT, the enzyme most specific to liver cells, is 28.5, inside the laboratory range but above the 25 ideal for women. Alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin and bile acids are all ideal and GLDH is normal, so this is not bile duct disease or liver cell damage; it is fat beginning to accumulate in the liver, which at 20 reverses completely. GGT is also the number that will confirm her plan is working before the scales do.

Her inflammatory marker hsCRP is 6.28 against a limit of 1.0. In the absence of a current infection, the most likely driver at 20 is excess body fat, which is itself inflammatory, with insulin resistance behind it. Her white cell count, neutrophils and monocytes all sit in the upper part of their ranges in keeping with that, while IL-8, the messenger that recruits neutrophils to bacterial infection, is at the bottom of its range, which argues against an active infection at the time of the draw. Her raised IgE, eczema and hand pain could each add a little to the CRP. Because new joint pain in the hands with a CRP at this level deserves a proper look even when the autoimmune screen is negative, we would recommend her GP repeats the CRP when she is well, and if it stays above 5 refers her to be examined.

Immunity is the theme behind her year of infections, and the antibody results are reassuring in that she is not short of them: IgG, IgA and IgM are all normal, and the coeliac test is valid because IgA is not deficient. What she is short of is zinc. At 9.2 against a limit of 10.7 and an ideal of 12 or more, zinc is low, and zinc is central to immune defence, skin repair and healing. Low zinc is associated with recurrent infections, slow healing, acne and dermatitis, which reads like her list. Copper, which competes with zinc, is 32.1 against a limit of 24.4. The combined pill raises copper reliably because oestrogen increases its carrier protein, and that is almost certainly the cause, but a high copper next to a low zinc widens the gap between them in a way that is associated with inflammation and poorer immune function. Her IgE is 104.5 against a limit of 100, with a basophil count marginally above range at 0.08, and together these confirm a mild allergic tendency behind the eczema and dermatitis. Vitamin D is 74, a whisker below the 75 ideal floor in a September sample, and it will fall through the winter without support. B12 is 359 with an active B12 of 58, both inside the range but below ideal, and a red cell size at the top of its ideal band fits that. Ferritin is 31 against an ideal of 40 or more, and with heavy periods and a CRP that inflates ferritin the true iron store is probably a little lower still; transferrin saturation of 19.8 percent, below the 25 percent ideal, says the same thing. Iron stores at this level do not cause anaemia but are associated with fatigue and poorer exercise tolerance.

Her hormones read as expected for someone on the combined pill: FSH, LH, oestradiol and progesterone are all suppressed because the pill switches off the signals from the brain to the ovaries, and this is not a fertility finding. Testosterone and the free androgen index are both ideal, which weighs against polycystic ovary syndrome as the explanation for the acne and weight gain and points back to insulin. Prolactin is 533 against a limit of 496. Sertraline is a well-recognised cause of a mild prolactin rise of exactly this size and the pill adds to it, so this is expected rather than alarming, but her GP should be aware because a persistent rise can affect periods, mood and libido and is worth a second sample taken rested. Her morning cortisol of 563 is inside the range but high in it; the pill raises the protein that carries cortisol, so the measured total goes up without more active hormone, though anxiety, poor sleep and pain all keep cortisol up and cortisol in turn worsens insulin resistance. Night sweats and hot flushes are recognised effects of sertraline, and a raised prolactin can contribute; nothing in the hormone panel points to an ovarian cause.

Her digestive results narrow the IBS question rather than answer it. H. pylori is negative, coeliac is negative, the pancreatic enzymes are ideal, and CA 125 is low. Gastrin is marginally below range at 4.96, which usually means the stomach is making acid normally and carries no concern. With those excluded, the two things in this report that most plausibly feed her bloating are the diet pattern behind the insulin resistance and the low zinc, which affects the gut lining.

The remaining findings are minor. Sodium at 146.2 and chloride at 108.2 are each a fraction above their limits, with a low urea, which reads as a morning sample from someone who had not drunk much rather than anything else. Bicarbonate at 18.1 is below the 20 limit; the commonest causes at her age are breathing faster when anxious, which lowers it, and a sample that sat before analysis, and with a normal anion gap and normal kidneys it is not an acid problem, though it is worth repeating once. Parathyroid hormone is 1.3 against a limit of 1.6 with an ideal calcium, which usually means the gland has nothing to do; not a concern now, but worth checking at her next test. HB-EGF, a growth factor, is above range, but that sample arrived at the wrong temperature and the result should not be read into. NGAL, a kidney injury marker, is below its range, which simply means there is no kidney stress.

Insulin resistance is the thread. A fasting insulin of 151 pmol/L (21.8 mIU/L), a C-peptide of 3.28, a HOMA-IR of 5.0 and an adiponectin of 2.07 are four views of the same process, and it explains the weight gain, the acne, the low HDL of 1.15, the triglycerides of 1.43, the raised GGT of 47.9, the ALT drifting above ideal, the SHBG sitting lower than it should on the pill, and most of the hsCRP of 6.28. The cholesterol picture, with an ApoB of 1.33 g/L and an LDL of 3.81, is the same story seen from the artery’s side, with the combined pill adding to it. Lp(a) is ideal and small dense LDL is close to ideal, so none of this is inherited and all of it is modifiable at 20.

Her immune year has a nutritional explanation running underneath it. Zinc at 9.2 is low, copper at 32.1 is high, vitamin D at 74 is a fraction below ideal, ferritin at 31 is below ideal with heavy periods, and B12 at 359 is adequate rather than abundant. Zinc and vitamin D both regulate the IgE pathway that is behind her eczema and dermatitis, zinc is needed for skin repair and wound healing, and a wide copper to zinc gap is associated with poorer immune function. The Epstein-Barr antibodies confirm past glandular fever, which is a fair contributor to a year of fatigue and vulnerability to infection. None of this is a deficiency in the sense of a disease, but taken together it is a body that has been running short of the things immunity is built from.

The joint pain in her hands is the finding that deserved the most careful exclusion, and the exclusion is good. Rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, ANA and C4 are all negative or normal, and the IL-17 family is low. With hypermobility already diagnosed, that is the most likely explanation, and the muscle enzymes CK and aldolase being normal argue against a muscle cause for her wider body pain. The one loose end is the hsCRP: inflammation from body fat is the probable driver, but a CRP above 5 alongside new joint pain should be repeated when she is well, and if it stays there she should be examined.

The prolactin of 533, the cortisol high in its range, the night sweats and the hot flushes all have sertraline and the combined pill as common threads. These are not reasons to stop either medication, which is a conversation for her prescriber, but they are worth raising together, because the pill is also contributing to the cholesterol and the copper, and there are contraceptive options that do not.
lifestyle:
Start with the honest picture: a diet rated 3 out of 10, high in refined carbohydrate and low in protein, is the single biggest reason her insulin is three times where it should be, and it is a long way from where it needs to be. It is also the lever that moves the most numbers in this report at once. None of the habits below need a diet plan; they attach to things she already does.
Put a palm-sized portion of protein on the plate first at every meal, before anything else. Eggs or Greek yoghurt at breakfast, chicken, fish, tofu, beans or cottage cheese later. Anchor: whatever she already eats stays, protein goes on the plate first. Why: protein at each meal blunts the insulin spike behind a fasting insulin of 151 and keeps her full for hours, which is what stops the weight gain.
Swap one white carbohydrate for a slow one, one meal at a time, starting with breakfast this week: oats or rye instead of cereal or white bread, then potatoes with skins, wholegrain rice or pasta at dinner the week after. Anchor: change breakfast only until it is automatic, then move to the next meal. Why: slower carbohydrate lowers the insulin her pancreas is over-producing, and with IBS a gradual change avoids a fibre shock.
Make sugary drinks and fruit juice a weekend-only thing, and put a bottle of water where the drinks used to be. Anchor: fill the water bottle when she makes her morning coffee. Why: liquid sugar goes straight to insulin and to the liver, and her GGT of 47.9 and sodium of 146 both point at what she drinks.
Walk for fifteen minutes straight after her biggest meal of the day. Anchor: plate in the sink, shoes on, out of the door. Why: a walk after eating flattens the glucose and insulin rise from that meal, which is the mechanism behind a HOMA-IR of 5.0, and it takes her steps from under 5,000 towards 7,000 without a gym.
Two short resistance sessions a week, twenty minutes each, bodyweight or light dumbbells, with a coach or physio who understands hypermobility for the first few sessions. Anchor: the same two days every week, after the post-meal walk. Why: muscle is where insulin does its work, and two sessions a week is the single most effective change for insulin resistance and for raising an HDL of 1.15. Hypermobility is a reason to do it well, not a reason to avoid it.
Fix the wake time, even at weekends, and get outside within an hour of waking. Anchor: alarm, then straight out with the water bottle. Why: a fixed wake time and morning light reset the sleep drive she is currently supplying with melatonin, and better sleep lowers the cortisol that sits high in her range and worsens insulin resistance.
Ten minutes of anything that slows breathing before bed: reading, stretching, a warm shower, no screen. Anchor: melatonin goes on the bedside table, and the ten minutes happen between taking it and lights out. Why: slower breathing is also the simplest fix for a bicarbonate of 18.1 that reads as anxious over-breathing, and it addresses the stress goal directly.

recommendations:
Hand joint pain with hsCRP 6.28: the autoimmune screen here (RF, anti-CCP, ANA, C4, IL-17) is negative, which is reassuring. Please repeat the CRP when she is well; if it is still above 5, an examination, and a hypermobility-informed physiotherapy referral either way.
Prolactin 533 against a limit of 496: a repeat sample taken rested, noting sertraline as the probable cause. If persistently raised, the post-PEG recovery test decides whether it is biologically active.
Insulin resistance at 20 (fasting insulin 21.8 mIU/L, HOMA-IR 5.0, adiponectin 2.07, HbA1c 38) with 20 kg gained in a year: worth documenting now so that a repeat in four months can show the direction of travel, and worth considering alongside the sertraline, which is associated with weight gain in some people.
The combined pill is contributing to her cholesterol (ApoB 1.33), copper (32.1), cortisol and prolactin, and she has heavy periods. A review of contraceptive options is reasonable.
Bicarbonate 18.1 and PTH 1.3 with a normal calcium: both to be repeated at the next test rather than acted on now.
Daytime fatigue on nightly melatonin, with past glandular fever confirmed on antibodies: worth a sleep conversation, since poor sleep raises both cortisol and insulin.
Targets: about 1,850 calories a day with 110 grams of protein and 30 grams of fibre built up over several weeks, aiming for 78 kg then 74 kg. Retest in four months. The markers that will show the plan is working, in the order they move: GGT, triglycerides, fasting insulin, hsCRP, HDL, ApoB.
supplementation:
Zinc picolinate 25 mg daily with food for three months, then 15 mg, taken away from iron. Zinc 9.2 is low and copper 32.1 is high; zinc supports immunity, skin repair and the gut lining, and narrows the copper to zinc gap.
Vitamin D3 2,000 IU daily with K2 through the winter, aiming to hold her level between 75 and 120. At 74 in September she will fall below 60 by February without it, and vitamin D helps regulate the IgE pathway behind her eczema.
Iron bisglycinate 25 mg every other day with vitamin C, away from zinc, to lift ferritin from 31 towards 60 given heavy periods. Recheck at four months and stop if ferritin is above 80.
Sublingual methylcobalamin 1,000 mcg daily for three months. B12 of 359 ng/L with an active B12 of 58 is adequate rather than abundant, and tiredness is her complaint.
Magnesium glycinate 300 mg in the evening. Her serum level is only just inside ideal, magnesium improves insulin sensitivity and sleep, and the glycinate form is gentle on IBS.
Omega-3 fish oil providing 2 grams of EPA and DHA daily, with a meal, for the triglycerides of 1.43 and the inflammatory picture.
Berberine 500 mg twice daily with meals is an evidence-based option for insulin resistance at her age, but it interacts with some medications and must be cleared with her prescriber first because she takes sertraline and guanfacine.
Do not take a multivitamin containing copper, or any thyroid support: copper is already high and the thyroid is working well.
The most important changes are not supplements. They are protein at every meal, slower carbohydrate, two to three resistance sessions a week, a daily walk, and a conversation with her GP about the pill and the prolactin.

biomarkers.name: TrueScore
biomarkers.description: Your TrueScore is 84 out of 100. Every marker is scored on how far it sits from its ideal range, combined by body system with the systems that matter most for long-term health weighted highest, and then capped by the most serious finding, so a result that needs a GP cannot be hidden by good numbers elsewhere. Raw weighted score 84.1; capped below 85 while a system is rated "Needs attention"; final 84.
biomarkers.low_causes: One or more systems needing a GP, several sub-optimal systems

biomarkers.name: PhenoAge
biomarkers.description: PhenoAge is a biological age estimated from nine blood markers (Levine 2018). Randox does not report red cell distribution width, one of the nine, so a typical value of 13 percent was used for that input; the effect on the result is under a year either way. It sits above her calendar age of 20 because of the hsCRP, glucose and white cell count, and it will fall as the insulin resistance and inflammation resolve.
biomarkers.high_causes: Inflammation, raised glucose, anaemia, kidney or liver strain, smoking

biomarkers.name: Cardiovascular Risk Score
biomarkers.description: The Cardiovascular Risk Score is a TrueVitals index from 0 to 100 built from ApoB, LDL, HDL, triglycerides, Lp(a), hsCRP and HbA1c, where 20 or below is ideal and 40 or below is acceptable. It deliberately ignores age, so it shows the risk being built rather than the risk already realised. At 85 it is high, driven by the ApoB of 1.33, the HDL of 1.15 and the hsCRP of 6.28. Her ten-year chance of an event is still very low because she is 20; this score is the reason to act now so that it stays that way. Every input except Lp(a) is modifiable, and Lp(a) is the one that is fine.
biomarkers.high_causes: Raised ApoB or LDL, high Lp(a), inflammation, raised HbA1c, smoking

biomarkers.name: Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT)
biomarkers.description: ALT is the enzyme most specific to liver cells. At 28.5 it is within the laboratory range but above the 25 ideal for women. At 20, with a GGT above range and insulin resistance, a mildly raised ALT most often reflects fat beginning to accumulate in the liver. It is early and fully reversible.

biomarkers.name: Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)
biomarkers.description: ALP comes from liver, bone and gut. At 76 it is within range and ideal, and a normal ALP alongside a raised GGT rules out a bile duct problem.

biomarkers.name: Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST)
biomarkers.description: AST is a liver and muscle enzyme. Below 18.7 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Gamma-Glutamyltransferase (GGT)
biomarkers.description: GGT is the most sensitive liver enzyme to metabolic strain, alcohol and some medications. At 47.9 it is above the 42 limit and nearly double the ideal. Lara does not drink heavily, and her pattern of insulin resistance, weight gain and a rising ALT points to fat in the liver as the driver. The combined pill and some medications can nudge GGT too. GGT tracks weight loss closely, and it is the number that will confirm her plan is working before anything else does.

biomarkers.name: Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)
biomarkers.description: LDH is released from many tissues when cells turn over. At 265 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Glutamate Dehydrogenase (GLDH)
biomarkers.description: GLDH is an enzyme from the centre of liver cells that rises with liver cell injury. At 4.0 it is within range, so the GGT rise is not accompanied by cell damage.

biomarkers.name: Total Bilirubin
biomarkers.description: Bilirubin is the yellow pigment from red cell breakdown, cleared by the liver. At 6.38 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Direct Bilirubin
biomarkers.description: Direct bilirubin is the form the liver has processed. At 1.83 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Bile Acids
biomarkers.description: Bile acids reflect bile flow. At 2.60 they are ideal.

biomarkers.name: Albumin
biomarkers.description: Albumin is the main protein the liver makes and a marker of nutrition and liver capacity. At 44.1 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Globulin
biomarkers.description: Globulins are the antibody and transport proteins. At 31.8 they are within range and at the top of the ideal band, in keeping with an immune system that has been busy this year.

biomarkers.name: Aldolase
biomarkers.description: Aldolase is a muscle enzyme that rises with muscle inflammation. At 5.88 it is within range, which with a normal CK argues against an inflammatory muscle cause for her pain.

biomarkers.name: Pancreatic Amylase
biomarkers.description: Pancreatic amylase is the digestive enzyme for starch. At 29 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Lipase
biomarkers.description: Lipase is the digestive enzyme for fat. At 40.5 it is ideal, so her digestive symptoms are not coming from the pancreas.

biomarkers.name: A/G Ratio
biomarkers.description: The albumin to globulin ratio compares the liver’s main protein with the antibody proteins. At 1.39 it is within range and ideal.

biomarkers.name: Liver Assessment
biomarkers.description: GGT 47.9 above range, ALT above ideal, FIB-4, APRI and NAFLD fibrosis score all low, bilirubin and bile acids ideal. Reversible.
biomarkers.result: Early fatty liver pattern, no scarring

biomarkers.name: FIB-4 Index
biomarkers.description: FIB-4 estimates liver scarring from age, platelets, ALT and AST. At 20 with these values it is very low, so the GGT rise is not accompanied by any scarring.

biomarkers.name: APRI
biomarkers.description: APRI is a second liver scarring index built from AST and platelets. Very low; no scarring.

biomarkers.name: NAFLD Fibrosis Score
biomarkers.description: The NAFLD fibrosis score estimates scarring in fatty liver disease. Firmly in the low-risk band, which is what an early, reversible fatty liver pattern looks like.
biomarkers.high_causes: Advanced fibrosis in fatty liver disease

biomarkers.name: AST:ALT Ratio (De Ritis)
biomarkers.description: The De Ritis ratio compares AST to ALT. A ratio below 1 with a raised GGT points to metabolic rather than alcohol-related liver strain.
biomarkers.high_causes: Alcohol-related liver disease, cirrhosis, muscle injury

biomarkers.name: R Factor
biomarkers.description: The R factor compares the ALT pattern with the ALP pattern to say whether liver strain is in the cells or the bile ducts. At 0.82 it is low, which with the GGT points to a mild metabolic, fat-related pattern rather than a bile duct one.

biomarkers.name: Total Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Total cholesterol is the sum of all cholesterol-carrying particles. At 5.61 it is above the 5.0 limit. Cholesterol at 20 is unusual enough to explain: it is driven here by weight gain, insulin resistance and the combined pill, all of which raise LDL, rather than by anything she was born with. The particle count (ApoB) is the number to act on.

biomarkers.name: LDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: LDL is the cholesterol carried in the particles that deposit in artery walls. At 3.81 it is above the 3.0 limit and well above the 2.6 ideal. At 20 this is almost entirely modifiable. Lipoprotein (a) and small dense LDL are both fine, so the excess is in ordinary LDL, which responds to weight loss, fibre, less refined carbohydrate and, in time, a review of the contraceptive with her GP.

biomarkers.name: HDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: HDL is the cholesterol carried in particles that remove cholesterol from tissues. At 1.15 it is below the 1.55 limit and further below the 1.6 ideal for women. Low HDL is a classic feature of insulin resistance and low activity, which is exactly the pattern in her insulin and adiponectin results. HDL rises with regular exercise, weight loss and less sugar more reliably than with any supplement.

biomarkers.name: Total Cholesterol / HDL Cholesterol Ratio
biomarkers.description: The ratio of total to HDL cholesterol. At 4.88 it is within the laboratory range but far above the 3.5 ideal, because HDL is low and LDL is high at the same time. This ratio improves fastest when both move.

biomarkers.name: Triglycerides
biomarkers.description: Triglycerides are the fat particles in the blood between meals. At 1.43 they are within range but above the 1.0 ideal. Raised triglycerides with a low HDL is the signature of insulin resistance and refined carbohydrate, and her TG to HDL ratio confirms it.

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein A-I
biomarkers.description: ApoA-I is the main protein on HDL particles. At 112 it is within range but below the ideal, mirroring the low HDL.

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein B
biomarkers.description: ApoB is the protein on every artery-damaging particle, so it counts the particles rather than the cholesterol inside them. At 133 mg/dl, which is 1.33 g/L, it is within the laboratory range but far above the ideal of 0.8 g/L. This is the single number that best captures her cardiovascular risk, and it is high for 20. It is also the number most likely to fall with weight loss and better insulin sensitivity.

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein B / A-I Ratio
biomarkers.description: The ratio of artery-damaging particles to protective ones. At 1.19 it is above the 0.90 limit and double the 0.6 ideal for women. It is high because ApoB is high and ApoA-I is low at the same time. Everything that improves insulin resistance improves this ratio.

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein E
biomarkers.description: ApoE is a transport protein involved in clearing fat particles from the blood. At 3.42 it is within range. This is the protein level, not the genetic type.

biomarkers.name: Small LDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Small dense LDL are the LDL particles most likely to lodge in artery walls. At 36.6 it is within range and only slightly above ideal. Her LDL excess is mostly in the larger, less harmful particles, which is genuinely good news given the LDL level.

biomarkers.name: Lipoprotein (a)
biomarkers.description: Lp(a) is an inherited cholesterol particle that raises heart risk independently of diet and does not change with lifestyle. At 30.4 nmol/L it is within the ideal range. This is worth knowing once: it means her cholesterol problem is acquired, not inherited, and is therefore fixable.

biomarkers.name: Homocysteine
biomarkers.description: Homocysteine is an amino acid that rises when B12, folate or B6 are short and damages blood vessels when high. At 6.0 it is ideal, so B vitamin metabolism is keeping up despite the B12 being below ideal.

biomarkers.name: TG/HDL Ratio
biomarkers.description: The triglyceride to HDL ratio is a reliable stand-in for insulin resistance and small dense LDL. At 1.24 it is within range but above the 0.87 ideal, which agrees with the insulin and adiponectin results.

biomarkers.name: Remnant Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Remnant cholesterol is the cholesterol carried in triglyceride-rich particles, and it damages arteries independently of LDL. At 0.65 it is within range but above the 0.5 ideal, driven by the triglycerides.

biomarkers.name: Lp(a)-Corrected LDL
biomarkers.description: LDL with the Lp(a) contribution removed shows how much of the LDL is modifiable. Almost all of it is.
biomarkers.high_causes: Diet high in saturated fat, familial hypercholesterolaemia

biomarkers.name: Atherogenic Index of Plasma
biomarkers.description: The atherogenic index of plasma is derived from triglycerides and HDL and predicts small dense LDL. Above ideal, driven by the low HDL.
biomarkers.high_causes: High triglycerides, low HDL, insulin resistance

biomarkers.name: LDL:HDL Ratio (Castelli II)
biomarkers.description: Castelli risk index II is LDL divided by HDL. Above ideal because LDL is high and HDL low at the same time.

biomarkers.name: Non-HDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Non-HDL cholesterol is everything except the protective HDL, so it captures every artery-damaging particle. At 4.46 it is above the 3.8 limit and the 3.0 ideal, in step with the ApoB.

biomarkers.name: HDL % of Total
biomarkers.description: HDL as a share of total cholesterol. At 20.5 percent it is at the bottom of the range and below ideal, because HDL is low and total is high.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low HDL or high total cholesterol

biomarkers.name: Castelli Risk Index I
biomarkers.description: Castelli index I is total cholesterol divided by HDL. At 4.88 it is within range but above the 3.5 ideal.

biomarkers.name: Atherogenic Coefficient
biomarkers.description: The atherogenic coefficient is non-HDL cholesterol divided by HDL. At 3.88 it is above the 3.0 limit, driven by a high non-HDL and a low HDL together.

biomarkers.name: VLDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: VLDL is estimated from triglycerides and carries them out of the liver. At 0.65 it is within range but above ideal.

biomarkers.name: LDL:HDL Ratio
biomarkers.description: LDL:HDL Ratio is calculated from your measured results. It sits outside the ideal range. It is being driven by LDL Cholesterol, which sits outside the ideal range.

biomarkers.name: LDL Particle Count (estimated)
biomarkers.description: LDL particle number estimated from ApoB, one particle per ApoB molecule. At about 1330 nmol/L it is above the 1300 limit, the particle-count view of the ApoB result.

biomarkers.name: Small LDL % of Total LDL
biomarkers.description: The share of LDL carried in small dense particles. At 24.8 percent it is within range and just inside ideal: her LDL is mostly the larger, less harmful kind.

biomarkers.name: Glucose
biomarkers.description: Fasting glucose is the sugar in the blood before eating. At 5.21 it is within the laboratory range but above the 5.0 ideal for someone her age. On its own this would not concern anyone. Next to an insulin of 151 it tells a different story: the pancreas is having to produce a great deal of insulin to hold glucose at this level. That effort is the definition of insulin resistance, and it is the thread that ties together her weight gain, low HDL, raised triglycerides, low adiponectin and raised GGT.

biomarkers.name: HbA1c
biomarkers.description: HbA1c is average blood sugar over the past three months. At 38 it is below the 42 limit but above the 36 ideal, sitting in the zone that tends to drift into prediabetes over the following years if insulin resistance is not addressed. At 20 that drift is entirely reversible.

biomarkers.name: Insulin
biomarkers.description: Fasting insulin is the hormone that moves sugar out of the blood, and a high fasting level means the body is having to shout to be heard. At 151 pmol/L, which is 21.8 mIU/L, it is within the laboratory range but nearly three times the ideal ceiling of 8 mIU/L. A HOMA-IR calculated from this and her glucose comes to 5.0, where below 1.5 is ideal. Insulin at this level drives fat storage, appetite, acne, low HDL and inflammation, and it explains 20 kilograms of weight gain in a year far better than willpower does. This is the finding to build her plan around.

biomarkers.name: Non-Esterified Fatty Acids
biomarkers.description: NEFA are free fatty acids released from fat stores. At 0.40 they are within range and ideal.

biomarkers.name: C-peptide
biomarkers.description: C-peptide is produced in equal amounts to insulin and is a steadier measure of how hard the pancreas is working. At 3.28 it is within the laboratory range but above the 2.5 ideal, confirming the fasting insulin: high insulin output to compensate for insulin resistance.

biomarkers.name: Fructosamine
biomarkers.description: Fructosamine reflects average blood sugar over the past two to three weeks. At 224 it is ideal, consistent with the HbA1c.

biomarkers.name: Adiponectin
biomarkers.description: Adiponectin is a hormone made by fat tissue that makes the body more sensitive to insulin and calms inflammation. It falls as visceral fat rises. At 2.07 it is below the 3.81 limit and a long way below ideal. Low adiponectin is one of the earliest and most sensitive signals of metabolically unhealthy weight gain, and it rises again with weight loss, exercise and sleep. This result and the insulin are two views of the same problem.

biomarkers.name: Metabolic Assessment
biomarkers.description: Fasting insulin 151 pmol/L (21.8 mIU/L), C-peptide 3.28, HOMA-IR 5.0, adiponectin 2.07, HbA1c 38. Glucose still controlled at the cost of very high insulin output. The central finding of this report.

biomarkers.name: Estimated Average Glucose
biomarkers.description: Average glucose estimated from HbA1c. Above ideal, consistent with early insulin resistance.

biomarkers.name: TyG Index
biomarkers.description: The TyG index combines triglycerides and glucose as a marker of insulin resistance. Above ideal, agreeing with HOMA-IR.

biomarkers.name: HOMA-IR
biomarkers.description: HOMA-IR estimates insulin resistance from fasting glucose and insulin together. At 5.03 it is above the 2.5 limit and more than three times the ideal of 1.5. This is the clearest single statement of insulin resistance on the panel and the number the plan is built around. Calculated from glucose 5.21 and insulin 21.7 mIU/L; Randox’s own value is pending and will replace it when it arrives.

biomarkers.name: HOMA-B
biomarkers.description: HOMA-B estimates how hard the insulin-producing cells are working. At 254 percent it is above the laboratory range, which means the pancreas is compensating for resistance by over-producing. Beta cells can keep this up for years, but the earlier the demand is reduced the better.

biomarkers.name: Glucose:Insulin Ratio
biomarkers.description: The glucose to insulin ratio, in mg/dL per mIU/L, falls as insulin resistance rises. At 4.3 it is below the 4.5 limit, agreeing with HOMA-IR that insulin resistance is present.

biomarkers.name: Adiponectin:Insulin Ratio
biomarkers.description: The adiponectin to insulin ratio combines the two most sensitive markers of metabolically unhealthy weight. At 0.10 it is well below the 0.3 limit: low adiponectin and high insulin at the same time.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low adiponectin with high insulin, metabolically unhealthy weight

biomarkers.name: High Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hsCRP)
biomarkers.description: hsCRP measures low-grade inflammation throughout the body. At 6.28 it is above the 1.0 limit and six times the ideal. In the absence of a current infection, a value like this at 20 is most often driven by excess body fat, which is itself inflammatory, and by insulin resistance. Her raised IgE, eczema, hand joint pain and a year of recurrent infections could each add to it. The autoimmune markers being negative makes an inflammatory arthritis less likely, but with new hand joint pain this level should be repeated by her GP once she is well, and if it stays above 5 it needs a proper look.

biomarkers.name: Antistreptolysin O (ASO)
biomarkers.description: ASO detects antibodies from a recent streptococcal throat or skin infection. Below 28 it is negative, so her recurrent throat infections were not streptococcal in the recent past.

biomarkers.name: D-Dimer
biomarkers.description: D-dimer is a breakdown product of blood clots. At 0.165 it is within range and ideal, with no sign of abnormal clotting. Worth noting because the combined pill raises clotting risk.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin-5 (IL-5)
biomarkers.description: IL-5 is a messenger that drives eosinophils in allergic responses. At 0.29 it is within range. The sample for this and the other interleukins arrived outside its stability window, which is only worth knowing because these are fragile proteins; the values are reported as received.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin-8 (IL-8)
biomarkers.description: IL-8 recruits neutrophils to sites of inflammation. At 5.27 it is at the very bottom of the range, which argues against an active bacterial process at the time of the draw.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin-15 (IL-15)
biomarkers.description: IL-15 supports natural killer and memory T cells. At 1.07 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Epidermal Growth Factor (EGF)
biomarkers.description: EGF drives skin and gut lining repair. At 52 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Heparin-binding EGF-like growth factor (HB-EGF)
biomarkers.description: HB-EGF is a growth factor involved in tissue repair and blood vessel remodelling. At 167 it is above the 136 limit, but this sample arrived at the wrong temperature and HB-EGF is temperature sensitive, so this one result should not be read into. It can be repeated if there is ever a reason to.

biomarkers.name: Monocyte Chemotactic Protein-1 (MCP-1)
biomarkers.description: MCP-1 draws monocytes into fat tissue and artery walls and rises with excess body fat. At 197 it is within range and within ideal, which is one inflammatory pathway that is not yet switched on.

biomarkers.name: Granulocyte Macrophage Colony Stimulating Factor (GM-CSF)
biomarkers.description: GM-CSF stimulates production of white cells. At 0.37 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin 17A
biomarkers.description: IL-17A is the messenger behind psoriasis-type and some joint inflammation. At 0.09 it is low, which is reassuring with her hand joint pain.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin 17F
biomarkers.description: IL-17F works alongside IL-17A. At 0.08 it is low.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin 22
biomarkers.description: IL-22 protects the gut and skin barrier. At 1.66 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: NLR
biomarkers.description: The neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio is a simple measure of inflammatory load. At 2.08 it is within range and marginally above the ideal ceiling of 2.0, consistent with the low-grade inflammation seen on hsCRP rather than with an acute infection.

biomarkers.name: Inflammation Assessment
biomarkers.description: hsCRP 6.28 against a limit of 1.0 with neutrophils and monocytes high in range, IL-8 at the bottom of range and IL-17 low. Reads as inflammation from excess body fat and insulin resistance rather than infection or autoimmunity. Repeat when well.

biomarkers.name: Platelet:Lymphocyte Ratio
biomarkers.description: The platelet to lymphocyte ratio is a second inflammatory index. Within range.

biomarkers.name: Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index
biomarkers.description: The systemic immune-inflammation index combines neutrophils, platelets and lymphocytes. Above ideal, in keeping with the hsCRP.

biomarkers.name: Monocyte:HDL Ratio
biomarkers.description: The monocyte to HDL ratio links inflammatory cells to the lipoprotein that calms them. At 0.54 it is within range but above ideal, consistent with the low HDL and mild inflammation.

biomarkers.name: Total Protein
biomarkers.description: Total protein is albumin plus globulin. At 75.9 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Calcium (adjusted)
biomarkers.description: Calcium adjusted for albumin. At 2.35 it is ideal. This matters because her parathyroid hormone is low, and a normal calcium alongside a low PTH is the reassuring combination: the gland is quiet because calcium does not need defending.

biomarkers.name: Chloride
biomarkers.description: Chloride is an electrolyte that tracks sodium and hydration. At 108.2 it is marginally above the 108 limit, in step with the sodium, and both point to being slightly dehydrated on the morning of the draw rather than to anything else.

biomarkers.name: Magnesium
biomarkers.description: Magnesium is needed for hundreds of enzyme reactions, including insulin signalling, muscle relaxation and sleep. At 0.86 it is within the laboratory range and just inside the 0.85 ideal floor. Serum magnesium is a poor reflection of tissue stores, and with insulin resistance, IBS and chronic body pain there is a fair case for supporting it.

biomarkers.name: Phosphate
biomarkers.description: Phosphate works with calcium in bone and energy metabolism. At 0.95 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Potassium
biomarkers.description: Potassium governs nerve and muscle electrical activity. At 4.28 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Sodium
biomarkers.description: Sodium is the main electrolyte in blood and the best simple gauge of hydration. At 146.2 it is marginally above the 146 limit. With chloride marginally up too and urea low, this reads as a morning sample from someone who had not drunk much, and it is not a kidney or hormone problem.

biomarkers.name: Bicarbonate
biomarkers.description: Bicarbonate is the blood’s main buffer against acid. At 18.1 it is below the 20 limit. The commonest causes at her age are breathing a little fast when anxious, which blows off carbon dioxide and lowers bicarbonate, and a sample that sat before analysis. With a normal anion gap and normal kidneys this is not a metabolic acid problem. It is worth repeating once with her GP if it is still low next time.

biomarkers.name: Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)
biomarkers.description: PTH is the hormone that raises blood calcium when it falls. At 1.3 it is below the 1.6 limit. With calcium ideal and vitamin D adequate, a low PTH usually means the gland has nothing to do rather than that it is failing. It is not a concern, but it is one to keep an eye on at her next test, because a persistently suppressed PTH with a drifting calcium would need a closer look.

biomarkers.name: Dickkopf-1 (DKK-1)
biomarkers.description: DKK-1 is a regulator of bone formation. At 2610 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Anion Gap
biomarkers.description: The anion gap checks whether a low bicarbonate is due to an unmeasured acid. At 24.2 it is above range, but this figure is inflated by the marginally high sodium and chloride and the low bicarbonate from the same slightly dehydrated, possibly delayed sample; corrected for albumin it is 23.8. With normal kidneys, normal glucose, no ketones in the urine and a normal lactate dehydrogenase, there is no acid process behind it, and the right response is a repeat rather than concern.

biomarkers.name: Bone Assessment
biomarkers.description: Adjusted calcium 2.35, phosphate 0.95, DKK-1 within range, vitamin D 74. PTH 1.3 below range with an ideal calcium, to recheck rather than act on.

biomarkers.name: Glucose-Corrected Sodium
biomarkers.description: Sodium corrected for glucose. Glucose is near normal so the correction is small; the marginal sodium stands, and reflects hydration.

biomarkers.name: Calculated Serum Osmolality
biomarkers.description: Calculated serum osmolality reflects the concentration of the blood. Slightly high, consistent with the marginal sodium and a morning sample taken without much fluid.
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, high sodium intake, raised glucose or urea

biomarkers.name: Albumin-Corrected Anion Gap
biomarkers.description: Anion gap corrected for albumin. Inflated by the same sample effects as the anion gap and not a sign of an acid process.
biomarkers.high_causes: Dietary acid load, reduced kidney clearance, ketosis, dehydration

biomarkers.name: Calcium:Phosphate Ratio
biomarkers.description: The calcium to phosphate ratio reflects mineral balance. At 2.47 it is within the ideal range.

biomarkers.name: Microalbumin / Creatinine Ratio
biomarkers.description: The urine albumin to creatinine ratio detects the earliest leak of protein through the kidney filters. At 0.8 it is ideal, so insulin resistance and inflammation have not touched the kidneys.

biomarkers.name: Creatinine
biomarkers.description: Creatinine is a muscle waste product cleared by the kidneys. At 57.6 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Cystatin C
biomarkers.description: Cystatin C is a filtration marker that is not affected by muscle mass and is more reliable than creatinine. At 0.89 it is within range and within ideal.

biomarkers.name: Beta-2-Microglobulin
biomarkers.description: Beta-2-microglobulin is a small protein cleared by the kidneys that also rises with immune activation. At 1.69 it is within range and ideal.

biomarkers.name: Urea
biomarkers.description: Urea is a protein waste product cleared by the kidneys. At 3.08 it is ideal and suggests her protein intake is modest.

biomarkers.name: Uric Acid
biomarkers.description: Uric acid is a waste product that rises with insulin resistance, fructose and alcohol. At 222 it is ideal, which is a pleasant surprise given the insulin picture.

biomarkers.name: Neutrophil Gelatinase-Associated Lipocalin (NGAL)
biomarkers.description: NGAL rises with acute kidney injury. At 436 it is below the laboratory range, which carries no clinical concern: a low NGAL simply means there is no kidney stress. It is reported as it was received.

biomarkers.name: Kidney Assessment
biomarkers.description: Cystatin C 0.89, eGFR 129, no urine albumin. Nothing to act on.

biomarkers.name: eGFR (Creatinine)
biomarkers.description: eGFR from creatinine alone, as reported by Randox. At 129 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: eGFR (Cystatin C)
biomarkers.description: eGFR estimated from cystatin C, which is unaffected by muscle mass. Ideal.
biomarkers.low_causes: Chronic kidney disease, dehydration, kidney strain

biomarkers.name: eGFR (Creatinine + Cystatin C)
biomarkers.description: eGFR combining creatinine and cystatin C, the most accurate estimate available. Ideal.
biomarkers.low_causes: Chronic kidney disease, dehydration, kidney strain

biomarkers.name: Urea:Creatinine Ratio
biomarkers.description: The urea to creatinine ratio helps separate hydration and diet from kidney disease. Within the expected range.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low protein intake, liver disease, overhydration
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, high protein intake, upper GI bleeding

biomarkers.name: Haemoglobin
biomarkers.description: Haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. At 135 it sits comfortably within the ideal range, which means the tiredness Lara describes is not being driven by anaemia. That matters because heavy periods are one of the commonest causes of low haemoglobin in women her age, and hers is holding up well.

biomarkers.name: Haematocrit
biomarkers.description: Haematocrit is the share of blood volume made up of red cells. At 40.8 percent it is ideal and consistent with the haemoglobin, so oxygen-carrying capacity is not a limiting factor for her energy.

biomarkers.name: Mean Cell Haemoglobin (MCH)
biomarkers.description: MCH is the average amount of haemoglobin inside each red cell. At 30.9 it is ideal. With heavy periods a falling MCH would be an early sign of iron running short, and there is no sign of that here.

biomarkers.name: Mean Cell Haemoglobin Concentration (MCHC)
biomarkers.description: MCHC is how concentrated the haemoglobin is within each cell. At 331 it is ideal, so red cells are being built with enough iron.

biomarkers.name: Red Blood Cell Mean Cell Volume (MCV)
biomarkers.description: MCV is the average size of a red cell. At 93.4 it is within the laboratory range and only just above the ideal band. Slightly larger cells can hint that B12 or folate are not fully abundant, which fits her B12 sitting below its ideal level.

biomarkers.name: Red Blood Cell Count
biomarkers.description: The number of red cells per litre. At 4.37 it is ideal for a woman her age.

biomarkers.name: Basophil Count
biomarkers.description: Basophils are a small population of white cells involved in allergic and histamine responses. At 0.08 the count is marginally above the 0.06 limit. At this level and alongside a raised IgE, eczema and dermatitis, it reads as part of an allergic-type tendency rather than anything sinister, and on its own it needs no action.

biomarkers.name: Eosinophil Count
biomarkers.description: Eosinophils rise with allergy and parasites. At 0.10 they are ideal, which is a useful counterpoint to the IgE and basophil findings: the allergic tendency is mild.

biomarkers.name: Lymphocyte Count
biomarkers.description: Lymphocytes are the white cells that hold immune memory and fight viruses. At 2.70 they are within the laboratory range and only slightly above the ideal band, which can follow a year of repeated infections.

biomarkers.name: Monocyte Count
biomarkers.description: Monocytes are the white cells that clear up after infection and inflammation. At 0.62 they are within range but sit in the upper part, consistent with the low-grade inflammation seen on hsCRP.

biomarkers.name: Neutrophil Count
biomarkers.description: Neutrophils are the first-response white cells. At 5.61 they are within the laboratory range but above the ideal band. Chronic low-grade inflammation and higher body weight both push neutrophils up, and the pattern here fits the raised hsCRP rather than an active bacterial infection.

biomarkers.name: White Blood Cell Count
biomarkers.description: The total white cell count. At 9.11 it is within the laboratory range but close to the top of it. Taken with the neutrophils, monocytes and hsCRP, the immune system reads as being mildly and persistently switched on.

biomarkers.name: Platelet Count
biomarkers.description: Platelets are the cells that form clots. At 247 they are ideal. Platelets also rise with inflammation, so a normal count here is reassuring.

biomarkers.name: Iron
biomarkers.description: Serum iron is the iron in transit in the blood right now and swings with meals. At 14.3 it is ideal, though the more reliable picture comes from ferritin and transferrin saturation.

biomarkers.name: Ferritin
biomarkers.description: Ferritin is the stored form of iron and the best single measure of iron reserves. At 31 it is within the laboratory range but below the ideal level of 40 for a woman with heavy periods. Ferritin is also pushed up by inflammation, so with hsCRP at 6.28 the true stores are probably a little lower than 31 suggests. Iron stores in the 30s are enough to prevent anaemia but are associated with fatigue, poorer exercise tolerance and hair shedding. This is worth rebuilding.

biomarkers.name: Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC)
biomarkers.description: TIBC measures the capacity of the blood to carry iron. At 72.2 it is within range and slightly above ideal. The body raises its carrying capacity when stores are running low, so this small rise supports the picture of iron reserves that could be better.

biomarkers.name: Transferrin
biomarkers.description: Transferrin is the protein that carries iron. At 2.66 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Transferrin Saturation
biomarkers.description: Transferrin saturation is the share of the carrying protein that is actually loaded with iron. At 19.8 percent it is within range but below the ideal 25 to 40 percent, another sign that iron is available but not abundant.

biomarkers.name: Iron Status Assessment
biomarkers.description: Ferritin 31, transferrin saturation 19.8 percent and UIBC above ideal, with haemoglobin 135 ideal. Iron is available but not abundant, with heavy periods as the likely reason. Rebuild towards ferritin 60.

biomarkers.name: UIBC
biomarkers.description: Unsaturated iron binding capacity is the spare carrying capacity for iron. At 57.9 it is within range but above ideal, another sign that stores could be better.

biomarkers.name: Iron:TIBC Ratio
biomarkers.description: Iron divided by total binding capacity, the same quantity as transferrin saturation as a fraction. At 0.198 it is within range but below ideal.

biomarkers.name: Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1)
biomarkers.description: IGF-1 reflects growth hormone activity and tissue repair. At 34.6 it is ideal for 20.

biomarkers.name: Cortisol
biomarkers.description: Cortisol is the main stress hormone, measured here in the morning when it should be at its highest. At 563 it is within the laboratory range but above the ideal band. The combined pill raises the protein that carries cortisol, which pushes the measured total up without changing the active amount, so this reads as expected rather than as a stress finding. That said, she describes anxiety, poor sleep and pain, all of which keep cortisol high, and cortisol in turn worsens insulin resistance.

biomarkers.name: Follicle Stimulating Hormone
biomarkers.description: FSH drives egg development. At 2.13 it is low, which is exactly what the combined pill is designed to do: it switches off the signals from the brain to the ovaries. This is not a fertility finding while she is on the pill.

biomarkers.name: Luteinising Hormone
biomarkers.description: LH triggers ovulation. At 2.9 it is suppressed by the combined pill, as expected.

biomarkers.name: Prolactin
biomarkers.description: Prolactin is the pituitary hormone for milk production, and it rises with stress, sleep loss and several medications. At 533 it is above the 496 limit. Sertraline is a recognised cause of a mild prolactin rise of exactly this size, and the combined pill adds to it. A modest rise like this rarely needs anything beyond a repeat, but her GP should know, because prolactin above range can affect periods, mood and libido and a persistent rise is worth a second sample taken rested and away from breast stimulation.

biomarkers.name: Dehydroepiandrosterone Sulphate (DHEAs)
biomarkers.description: DHEA-S is the adrenal building block for sex hormones. At 7.3 it is ideal for her age.

biomarkers.name: Testosterone
biomarkers.description: Testosterone in women drives libido, muscle and mood. At 1.33 it is within range and ideal. Alongside a normal free androgen index this argues against polycystic ovary syndrome as the driver of her acne and weight gain, which points back to insulin.

biomarkers.name: Oestradiol
biomarkers.description: Oestradiol is the main oestrogen. At 113 it is low because the combined pill suppresses the ovaries and the synthetic oestrogen in the pill is not measured by this test. Expected, and not a concern.

biomarkers.name: Progesterone
biomarkers.description: Progesterone is the hormone of the second half of the cycle. At 0.89 it is low because the pill prevents ovulation. Expected.

biomarkers.name: Sex Hormone Binding Globulin
biomarkers.description: SHBG carries sex hormones in the blood and is raised by oestrogen and lowered by insulin resistance. At 54.5 it is within range and ideal. On the combined pill it is usually much higher, and the fact that it is not suggests insulin is holding it down, which is another quiet signal of insulin resistance.

biomarkers.name: Free Androgen Index
biomarkers.description: The free androgen index estimates active testosterone. At 2.44 it is ideal, which weighs against polycystic ovary syndrome.

biomarkers.name: Hormonal Assessment
biomarkers.description: FSH, LH, oestradiol and progesterone suppressed by the combined pill as expected. Testosterone and free androgen index ideal, weighing against PCOS. Prolactin 533 above range, most likely sertraline; GP to repeat.

biomarkers.name: Prolactin Recovery Post-PEG
biomarkers.description: Prolactin Recovery Post-PEG is part of the Signature panel but was reported by Randox as not available on this sample. This is the follow-on test that checks whether a raised prolactin is biologically active; it is the natural next step for the GP given the prolactin of 533.

biomarkers.name: Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH)
biomarkers.description: TSH is the pituitary signal that drives the thyroid. At 2.83 it is within the laboratory range but above the 2.5 ideal. With Free T4 and Free T3 both healthy and antibodies negative, the thyroid is working and this is not the cause of her weight gain. Worth watching rather than acting on.

biomarkers.name: Free Thyroxine (FT4)
biomarkers.description: FT4 is the storage form of thyroid hormone. At 14.7 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Free Tri-iodothyronine (FT3)
biomarkers.description: FT3 is the active thyroid hormone. At 5.67 it is ideal, and the FT3 to FT4 ratio shows conversion is working well.

biomarkers.name: Thyroid Assessment
biomarkers.description: FT4 14.7 and FT3 5.67 ideal, both antibodies negative, TSH 2.83 just above ideal. Not the cause of the weight gain or fatigue.

biomarkers.name: Thyroxine-Binding Globulin (TBG)
biomarkers.description: Thyroxine-Binding Globulin (TBG) is part of the Signature panel but was reported by Randox as not available on this sample. The free thyroid hormones were returned and are ideal, so its absence does not change the thyroid picture.

biomarkers.name: FT3:FT4 Ratio
biomarkers.description: The FT3 to FT4 ratio reflects how well the body converts thyroid hormone to its active form. Healthy.
biomarkers.low_causes: Poor T4 to T3 conversion, low ferritin or selenium, chronic illness

biomarkers.name: TSH:FT4 Ratio
biomarkers.description: The TSH to FT4 ratio rises when the pituitary has to work harder to keep thyroid output up. At 0.193 it is within range and just inside ideal.
biomarkers.high_causes: Pituitary working harder to maintain thyroid output

biomarkers.name: Copper
biomarkers.description: Copper is a trace mineral needed for iron use, energy and connective tissue. At 32.1 it is above the 24.4 limit. The combined pill reliably raises copper because oestrogen increases the copper-carrying protein, and that is almost certainly what this is. It still matters, because copper and zinc compete, and a high copper next to a low zinc widens the gap between them. That ratio is associated with inflammation, poorer immune function and skin problems, which is a fair description of her year.

biomarkers.name: Total Antioxidant Status (TAS)
biomarkers.description: TAS is a measure of the blood’s overall capacity to neutralise oxidative stress. At 1.68 it is within range and ideal.

biomarkers.name: Zinc
biomarkers.description: Zinc is needed for immune defence, wound healing, skin and taste. At 9.2 it is below the 10.7 limit and well below the 12 ideal. Low zinc is associated with recurrent infections, slow healing, acne and dermatitis, all of which she reports, and the combined pill and a high-carbohydrate diet both lower it. This is one of the most actionable results on the panel.

biomarkers.name: Folic acid
biomarkers.description: Folate is a B vitamin needed for cell division and red cell production. At 17.1 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Vitamin B12
biomarkers.description: B12 is needed for nerves, energy production and red cells. At 359 ng/L it is within the laboratory range but below the 500 ideal, and the active B12 tells the same story. B12 in this zone is associated with fatigue and low mood in some people, and a slightly large red cell size fits it. Worth bringing up.

biomarkers.name: Vitamin D
biomarkers.description: Vitamin D supports immunity, bone, mood and insulin sensitivity. At 74 it is within the laboratory range and a whisker below the 75 ideal floor. For a September sample this is good, but it will fall over winter without support, and immunity and mood are two of her priorities.

biomarkers.name: Active B12
biomarkers.description: Active B12 is the fraction of B12 that cells can actually use. At 58.2 it is within range but below the 70 ideal, confirming that total B12 is adequate rather than abundant.

biomarkers.name: B12 Status
biomarkers.description: B12 359 ng/L and active B12 58.2, both in range and below ideal. Intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies negative. Sublingual methylcobalamin recommended.

biomarkers.description: Zinc low, copper high, vitamin D, B12 and ferritin below ideal, magnesium at the ideal floor. Together they read as a body running short of what immunity and energy are built from, on a diet rated 3 out of 10.

biomarkers.name: Glutathione Reductase
biomarkers.description: Glutathione Reductase is part of the Signature panel but was reported by Randox as not available on this sample. It is the marker used to read riboflavin (B2) status, so B2 status could not be assessed on this sample.

biomarkers.name: Red Cell Folate
biomarkers.description: Reported by Randox as pending. Serum folate is ideal. This result will be added when it arrives.

biomarkers.name: Creatine Kinase-MB (CK-MB)
biomarkers.description: CK-MB is the heart-muscle form of creatine kinase. At 0.608 it is within range with no sign of heart muscle stress.

biomarkers.name: Creatine Kinase
biomarkers.description: Creatine kinase leaks from muscle when it is worked hard or damaged. At 52 it is ideal, consistent with a low training load. It also argues against a muscle cause for her body pain.

biomarkers.name: Myoglobin
biomarkers.description: Myoglobin is released from damaged muscle. Below 21 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Troponin T
biomarkers.description: Troponin T is the most specific marker of heart muscle injury. Below 3 it is undetectable, which is exactly right.

biomarkers.name: Fatty Acid Binding Protein-3 (FABP-3)
biomarkers.description: FABP-3 rises early after heart muscle strain. At 3.42 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Haemolysis Screen
biomarkers.description: Haptoglobin 1.469 within range and LDH 265 ideal. No sign of red cells breaking down.

biomarkers.name: Cardiac Risk Assessment
biomarkers.description: Troponin T undetectable, CK-MB, myoglobin and FABP-3 all within range. No sign of heart muscle stress. The cardiovascular risk sits in the lipids, not the heart muscle.

biomarkers.name: H. pylori
biomarkers.description: H. pylori antibodies detect the stomach bacterium associated with ulcers and reflux. At 0.63 the result is negative, which is one gastrointestinal cause of her bloating that can be set aside.

biomarkers.name: Gastrin
biomarkers.description: Gastrin is the hormone that tells the stomach to make acid. At 4.96 it is marginally below the 6 limit. A low gastrin usually means the stomach is producing acid normally and the hormone is not being called upon, and it carries no clinical concern.

biomarkers.name: Digestive Assessment
biomarkers.description: H. pylori negative, coeliac negative, pancreatic amylase and lipase ideal, gastrin marginally low with no concern. Her IBS symptoms are not explained by any of these, which leaves diet pattern and low zinc as the leads in this report.

biomarkers.name: Immunoglobulin E (IgE)
biomarkers.description: IgE is the antibody behind allergy and eczema. At 104.5 it is above the 100 limit and double the ideal. This fits the dermatitis, eczema and mild basophil rise, and it points to an atopic tendency. It is modest, not dramatic, and it does not explain the infections. Zinc and vitamin D both help regulate this pathway.

biomarkers.name: Complement Component 4 (C4)
biomarkers.description: C4 is part of the complement system that helps antibodies clear infection and falls in active lupus. At 0.355 it is within range, another argument against a connective tissue disease.

biomarkers.name: Haptoglobin
biomarkers.description: Haptoglobin binds free haemoglobin and falls when red cells are breaking down. At 1.469 it is within range, so there is no haemolysis.

biomarkers.name: Immunoglobulin A (IgA)
biomarkers.description: IgA is the antibody that guards the gut, airway and mucous membranes. At 1.82 it is within range. Importantly it is not deficient, which means the coeliac antibody test is valid.

biomarkers.name: Immunoglobulin G (IgG)
biomarkers.description: IgG is the main long-term antibody class. At 12.33 it is within range, so recurrent infections are not down to a lack of antibodies.

biomarkers.name: Immunoglobulin M (IgM)
biomarkers.description: IgM is the first antibody produced in a new infection. At 1.121 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Epstein-Barr Nuclear Antigen (EBNA) IgG
biomarkers.description: EBNA IgG appears months after Epstein-Barr infection and stays for life. At 96 it is strongly positive. This is the antibody pattern of past infection, and it confirms what Lara suspected: she has had glandular fever (mono). It is not an active infection now.

biomarkers.name: Epstein-Barr Viral Capsid Antigen (VCA) IgG
biomarkers.description: VCA IgG is the long-term memory antibody to Epstein-Barr virus. At 1969 it is strongly positive, consistent with a past infection. Very high VCA IgG with a positive EBNA and negative IgM is the standard picture of an infection that has passed, and it can stay this high for years.

biomarkers.name: Epstein-Barr Viral Capsid Antigen (VCA) IgM
biomarkers.description: VCA IgM appears in the first weeks of a new Epstein-Barr infection. At 0.238 it is negative. Combined with the positive IgG results, this rules out a current or very recent infection and confirms the mono was in the past. Fatigue after glandular fever can genuinely last a year, and that is a plausible contributor to her daytime tiredness.

biomarkers.name: Immune Assessment
biomarkers.description: IgG, IgA and IgM normal, so antibody production is not the problem behind a year of infections. Zinc 9.2 low and copper 32.1 high, IgE 104.5 above range, past Epstein-Barr infection confirmed.
biomarkers.result: Adequate antibodies, low zinc, allergic tendency

biomarkers.name: EBV Status
biomarkers.description: EBNA IgG 96.1 and VCA IgG 1969 positive, VCA IgM 0.238 negative. Glandular fever in the past, not active now. Post-viral fatigue can last a year.

biomarkers.name: Complement Component 3 (C3)
biomarkers.description: Complement Component 3 (C3) is part of the Signature panel but was reported by Randox as not available on this sample. C4 was returned and is normal, which covers the same question in part.

biomarkers.name: Neuron Specific Enolase (NSE)
biomarkers.description: NSE is a screening marker associated with neuroendocrine tumours. At 3.15 it is within range. Screening markers like this are reassuring when normal but are not diagnostic in either direction.

biomarkers.name: Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP)
biomarkers.description: AFP is a screening marker for liver and germ cell tumours. At 1.6 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA)
biomarkers.description: CEA is a screening marker associated with bowel cancer. At 1.1 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Cancer Antigen 15-3 (CA 15-3)
biomarkers.description: CA 15-3 is a screening marker associated with breast cancer. At 8.3 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Cancer Antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9)
biomarkers.description: CA 19-9 is a screening marker associated with pancreatic cancer. At 3.9 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Cancer Antigen 125 (CA 125)
biomarkers.description: CA 125 is a screening marker associated with ovarian cancer, and it also rises with endometriosis. At 5.8 it is within range and low, which sits comfortably alongside the MRI that found no endometriosis.

biomarkers.name: Human Chorionic Gonadotrophin (hCG)
biomarkers.description: hCG is the pregnancy hormone and a germ cell tumour marker. Below 0.2 it is negative.

biomarkers.name: Calcitonin
biomarkers.description: Calcitonin is a screening marker for medullary thyroid cancer. Below 0.5 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Cancer Screening Assessment
biomarkers.description: CEA, CA 19-9, CA 125, CA 15-3, AFP, NSE, hCG and calcitonin all within range. Screening support, not a diagnosis in either direction.

biomarkers.name: Mesothelin
biomarkers.description: Mesothelin is part of the Signature panel but was reported by Randox as not available on this sample. The other screening markers were returned and are all within range.

biomarkers.description: The Cardiovascular Risk Score of 85 out of 100 says the risk factors are present now: ApoB 1.33, HDL 1.15, hsCRP 6.28 and an HbA1c above ideal. Her ten-year chance of an event is very low because she is 20. Both statements are true, and the gap between them is the window for acting. Lp(a) is ideal, so nothing here is inherited.

biomarkers.description: Body mass index from her weight of 83 kg and height of 172 cm. At 28.1 it is above the 24.9 limit. After a gain of more than 20 kilograms in a year, it is the visible face of the insulin resistance in this report.
biomarkers.high_causes: Excess body fat or high muscle mass

biomarkers.name: Lean Body Mass (estimated)

biomarkers.name: Calorie Target
biomarkers.description: Around 1,850 calories a day, about 300 below her estimated expenditure, for steady fat loss of roughly half a kilogram a week without hunger.

biomarkers.name: Weight Target
biomarkers.description: About 74 kg brings her BMI to 25 and would be expected to normalise the insulin, adiponectin, GGT and HDL behind most of this report. A sensible first milestone is 78 kg.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Tissue Transglutaminase Antibodies (Coeliac)
biomarkers.description: The coeliac antibody. At 0.7 it is negative, which for someone with years of IBS and bloating is an important negative: coeliac disease is not the explanation, provided she was eating gluten at the time.

biomarkers.name: Rheumatoid Factor (RF)
biomarkers.description: Rheumatoid factor is an antibody found in most rheumatoid arthritis. Below 6.72 it is negative. With new hand joint pain this is a genuinely reassuring result, though a negative does not rule the condition out completely.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (Anti-CCP) Antibodies
biomarkers.description: Anti-CCP is the most specific antibody for rheumatoid arthritis and often appears years before symptoms. Below 8 it is negative. Together with the negative rheumatoid factor and low IL-17, this makes rheumatoid arthritis an unlikely cause of her hand pain, and hypermobility becomes the more probable explanation.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Nuclear Antibodies (ANA)
biomarkers.description: ANA is the screening antibody for lupus and related connective tissue conditions. Negative. With joint pain, fatigue, skin problems and a raised CRP, a negative ANA removes a whole family of diagnoses from the list.

biomarkers.name: Intrinsic Factor Antibodies
biomarkers.description: Intrinsic factor antibodies cause pernicious anaemia, a form of B12 deficiency. At 1.9 they are negative, so her below-ideal B12 is dietary or absorptive rather than autoimmune.

biomarkers.name: Gastric Parietal Cell Antibodies
biomarkers.description: Parietal cell antibodies are the second marker for autoimmune gastritis. At 0.70 they are negative.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Thyroglobulin Antibody (Anti-Tg)
biomarkers.description: Thyroglobulin antibodies signal autoimmune thyroid disease. At 17 they are negative.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Thyroid Peroxidase Antibody (Anti-TPO)
biomarkers.description: TPO antibodies are the main marker for Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Below 8 they are negative, so her thyroid is not under autoimmune attack, and thyroid can be crossed off the list of causes for weight gain and fatigue.

biomarkers.name: Autoimmune Assessment
biomarkers.description: ANA negative, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP negative, coeliac negative, thyroid, intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies negative, C4 normal. With new hand joint pain this is the reassuring result of the panel.
